subsystems.name: Probe array
subsystems.role: the tools that touch individual atoms — a single scanning probe tip can move atoms, but practical printing needs thousands working in parallel.
parts: ultra-sharp cantilever tips (silicon, or carbon nanotube)

subsystems.name: Tip chemistry and feedstock
subsystems.role: gives each tip a specific chemical job rather than just a push.
parts: precursor molecules (e.g. carbon monoxide, or reactive radicals)

subsystems.name: Positioning and metrology
subsystems.role: knowing exactly where every atom is, and proving it afterwards.
parts: ultra-high vacuum and often cryogenic cooling

subsystems.name: Workpiece
subsystems.role: the structure being built, plus the surface chemistry that makes sites reactive or inert on demand.
parts: growing lattice (silicon, diamond-like carbon, or a designed molecule)

subsystems.name: Design and control software
subsystems.role: turns a wanted object into a legal sequence of atomic placement moves.

buildSteps.title: Design the molecule and the route
buildSteps.detail: Computational chemistry is used to find reactions that place the desired atom and leave nothing unwanted behind — the hard part is chemistry, not machinery.

buildSteps.title: Prepare an atomically clean surface
buildSteps.detail: A flat crystal is cleaned in ultra-high vacuum and its surface atoms capped with hydrogen or another species so it is inert except where the tool works.

buildSteps.title: Park the tip
buildSteps.detail: Piezoelectric actuators bring a probe tip to a chosen site, with feedback keeping the gap stable; vibration and thermal drift of a fraction of an atom are the enemies.

buildSteps.title: Open one reactive site
buildSteps.detail: The tip plucks a single hydrogen atom, or otherwise activates one lattice position, leaving a dangling bond for a precursor molecule to bond to.

buildSteps.title: Deposit the atom or group
buildSteps.detail: A precursor is delivered to that site and the tip supplies energy or force to break and form specific bonds, leaving the atom locked in place.

buildSteps.title: Verify and correct
buildSteps.detail: The same tip images the result; misplaced atoms are removed and the step repeated.

buildSteps.title: Parallelise the writing
buildSteps.detail: Instead of one tip, an array of thousands writes identical patterns at once, the way research cantilever arrays already write in parallel — this is what turns a demonstration into manufacturing.

buildSteps.title: Build machines that build
buildSteps.detail: In the speculative end game, the printed structures are themselves molecular-scale assembly devices, so production copies itself and output grows exponentially. No such device has been demonstrated.

prerequisites.why: atoms have been positioned one at a time under a scanning probe since the late 1980s, though only in vacuum and at a crawl.
large cantilever arrays have been demonstrated for writing, but each tip is not yet a precise atomic tool.
credible, computed step-by-step reaction sequences for building rigid 3-D lattices are still mostly proposals.
without fast, non-destructive verification, error rates compound and a printed object is never trustworthy.
DNA origami and similar methods already build precise nanoscale shapes in bulk, far faster than any tip; combining the two is the most plausible route.

pathway.milestone: lab demonstrations of atom-by-atom writing, hydrogen-depassivation lithography on silicon, and bulk DNA origami
pathway.unlocks: proof that atoms can be placed deliberately, and that self-assembly can make precise shapes cheaply.

pathway.milestone: a small, functional device whose critical layer is made atom by atom
pathway.unlocks: atomically precise electronics, sensors and catalysts that are genuinely better than conventional ones.

pathway.milestone: hybrid production: self-assembly does the bulk, lithography defines the precise parts
pathway.unlocks: useful atomically precise materials at realistic cost and speed.
zero-waste, perfect-material manufacturing — highly speculative, and disputed among chemists over whether the required reactions are feasible outside a vacuum.
